en: The Mahāvaipulya Siṃhanāda Sūtra, translated by the Tripitaka Master Divākara of India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling in the Palace of the Sun and Moon, in the Hall of Supreme Treasures.
The Buddha was together with a great assembly of ninety hundred-thousand koṭis of bhikṣus, as well as immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Saṃbhadraka:

"To the north of here, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in sixty hundred-thousand nayutas of koṭis of Ganges sands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī. There, the Buddha named Dharmodgata Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently dwells and teaches the Dharma, establishing, sustaining, and pacifying all beings for their universal benefit."
"I now wish to expound the Mahāvaipulya, titled 'The Lion’s Roar,' which is difficult to encounter and difficult to hear; you should go there to listen to and receive its essential teachings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jayasthāman, having received the Buddha's instruction, immediately departed for the world of Sukhāvatī.
Upon seeing the Buddha Dharmodgata, he prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Buddha Dharmodgata, seeing the Bodhisattva Jyotīrasa, though already knowing [the answer], asked him intentionally, saying:
"O son of good family!
“From where have you come?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa remained seated with his mind focused, silent and without speech.
The entire great assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all had this thought:
“Vijayasambhava Bodhisattva!
Why do you remain silent and dwell with a mind of hesitation when asked by the Honored One of the Three Realms?

At that time, the Buddha, with his broad, luminous, and clear blue-lotus eyes, performed the lion’s stretch and gazed universally throughout the ten directions. Knowing the doubts of the great assembly, he manifested a smile and emitted a great golden light.
The light was intermingled with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various and diverse colors, universally illuminating the ten directions, while all the lands of the worlds shook violently.

At that time, the assemblies of Bodhisattvas from the ten directions, seeing this miraculous manifestation, came to the Buddha’s presence in their various forms and colors and diverse robes and garments; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and each sat upon a lotus throne, adorned by their own merit within the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*).

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vidyutprabhā rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and knelt with his right knee on the ground. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, filled with joy and a sense of wonder at such an unprecedented experience, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"In the past, I have witnessed immeasurable supernatural transformations, yet never before have I seen such radiance and an earthquake as what we behold now.
Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions: for what reason do you smile?"
"Please deign to show compassion and resolve the doubts of this assembly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vidyutkeśin addressed him with these verses:
"The Great Compassionate One, the Great Teacher, Does not smile without cause. [Please tell us] for what reason you have smiled."
“May the Buddha benefit sentient beings; out of compassion, please grant us a definitive teaching.

At that time, the Tathāgata Dharmodaya was majestic and radiant; his body shone with the brilliance of Jāmbūnada gold, emitting and pouring forth immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of subtle lights, like a great golden pillar.
The Bodhisattva Vidyut-mālā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have seen immeasurable supernatural powers and radiance, yet none such as today, which I have never beheld before.”
The Buddha told Vidyutprabhā: "So it is, so it is.
This great radiance and supernatural power of the Tathāgata appear rarely; he does not manifest this sign except for a great cause and condition."
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain to you the causes and conditions for my smile.
Do not be afraid, do not harbor other expectations, fortify your mind, and do not give rise to doubt.
Why is this? The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable; their power of vows and spiritual transformations are inconceivable.
Reflect deeply upon this and be careful not to harbor any doubt.
“Vidyutprabhā!
Do you see the Bodhisattva Jayoṣmāyatana, who has come as a messenger from Śākyamuni Buddha?
Vidyutprabhā replied:
“I see him.
“Good son! To this Bodhisattva Sañcaya, I asked:”
"From where have you come?
He remained silent in his mind and did not answer me.
It was because I saw this matter that I manifested a smile.
“The Tathāgata has questioned but not answered, and now this assembly has all given rise to doubt and wonder.
“Good son! The Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa has formed such an understanding:”
"All dharmas neither come nor go; why then, World-Honored One, do you ask me, 'From where have you come'?
Knowing that all dharmas are beyond verbal expression and that no location can be found, how could one speak of whence one has come?"
"Good son! This has been a brief explanation of the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas). Good son!"
Bodhisattva Vijayasamcaya!
Within all phenomena, there are no letters and no speech, because the nature of letters is transcended;
all phenomena have no emergence, because the nature of emergence is transcended.

All dharmas have no destination, for they proceed toward right abandonment; all dharmas have no manifestation, for they have nothing upon which to rely. They transcend mind, thought, and consciousness, and are detached from all causes and conditions.

They are nameless and wordless, without action and without demonstration. They pass beyond the paths of the eye and other senses, without accumulation, without birth, and detached from conceptualization. Having no location, they are detached from all locations. Dharmas consist of but a single syllable, namely, the "letterless" (*anakṣara*). Since they are fundamentally without speech, what could possibly be spoken?
“Good son! You should know that non-explanation is true explanation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Pure Body, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If that which is not spoken is true speaking, then should those who are mute and do not speak all be considered as preaching the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
"In this way, good son!
As you have said, it is not only those who are mute and silent who preach the Dharma; even those who are not mute and silent all preach the Dharma, yet they do not know the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhakāya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain clearly: in what way do all sentient beings preach the Dharma yet remain ignorant of the Dharma?"
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Viśuddhakāya: “Good son!

It is like a person born blind who dwells in the sunlight but does not see the sun; when others speak of it for him, it is only through the sound of another’s voice that he comes to know the sun exists.”

In this way, all phenomena enter the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm is without letters and is free from the nature of all letters. It cannot be expressed or discerned by sentient beings, yet it is spoken of through the power of causes and conditions.
It is like an echo in a deep valley: the valley itself is empty and soundless, yet because of causes and conditions, the sound of an echo arises.
In this same way, noble son, syllables and sounds manifest through the conjunction of causes and conditions, yet the realm of sentient beings is empty and devoid of syllables.
"Good son!
You should know that all the sounds and languages of sentient beings enter into the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge:
those who speak by means of words enter into the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid)."
That which is beyond verbal expression is the entrance into the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*);
that which analyzes through words is the entrance into the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*);
and that which accords with phenomena and resolves them without obstruction is the entrance into the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
One should know that all the verbal expressions of sentient beings are entirely subsumed within these four phrases of the Dharma.
The phrase of the meaning of reality is fundamentally immovable; it is like one born blind who, following the words of others, clings to what is not true vision as being real.
Therefore, son of good family!
Those who wish to seek the Dharma should seek it within themselves;
those who wish to seek bodhi should seek it within the five aggregates.
When these words of true meaning were spoken, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways and a great light shone everywhere.

The Buddha extended his broad and long tongue, which completely covered the trichiliocosm; from that tongue-mark he emitted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of rays of light, which illuminated all worlds from the great hells up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
He withdrew his broad and long tongue and addressed the great assembly:

“You should all know that the Tathāgata’s broad and long tongue was obtained through truthful speech; what the Tathāgata has spoken should be respectfully accepted and given rise to with true faith; do not harbor hesitation or give way to doubt.”

At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas of the ten stages, together with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and the entire great assembly, all rose from their seats and, joining their palms, spoke to the Buddha with one voice:
“We pray that the World-Honored One will explain the meaning of reality;
we pray that the Sugata will explain the meaning of reality.”
"We now desire only the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata and no other Dharma; we, this great assembly, are entirely free from doubt.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the entire great assembly twice and thrice, and spoke these words:

"Out of compassion for all the world, and for the sake of the benefit, peace, and happiness of many sentient beings, I have used the wealth of the Dharma to bring peace to gods and humans; therefore, I now utter the Great Lion’s Roar."
"Good sons!

You should know that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni of the Sahā world, who currently teaches the Dharma and establishes, sustains, and pacifies sentient beings, is none other than my Dharmodgata Tathāgata."
"In the Sahā world, I manifest various forms to benefit sentient beings, delivering them according to what is appropriate for each.
At that time, the great assembly, hearing these words, all felt a sense of wonder; they leaped for joy with unprecedented delight and cried out with one voice:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
The World-Honored One, wishing to cause all sentient beings to roar the lion’s roar, has therefore preached the true Dharma of the lion’s roar for this great assembly.

If anyone should hear it, you should know that such a person’s roots of goodness are not few; how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, widely proclaim, and disseminate it, or who offer respectful worship with various flower garlands, various garments, banners, streamers, canopies, and by burning, smearing, or grinding incense?
"Such a person shall be cherished and protected by all the Buddhas.
At that time, the Buddha praised the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! As you have said, the merit of these good sons and good daughters is not small.

Regarding this Dharma of the Buddha’s true lion’s roar, if anyone hears it with a pure mind and even once exclaims 'Excellent!', I shall protect and sustain them all, and they shall also be looked upon and summoned by Maitreya."

Such persons shall carry my bodhi upon their two shoulders; having received and believed in this sutra amidst the five turbidities, I shall bring them to maturity in every place of rebirth, and they shall also be protected by Maitreya.

This person shall be able to dry up the ocean of birth and death, subdue all Māras, and eliminate all afflictions; they shall beat the great Dharma drum, forever leave behind the female body, destroy all enmities and obstacles, and bring to rest the multitude of fetters.
If there are good sons or good daughters who, for as many eons as there are atoms in ten asaṃkhyeya trichiliocosms, provide and offer all manner of articles of pleasure to all Tathāgatas;

yet, upon hearing this sutra’s true supernatural powers, they harbor doubts and do not believe—such persons commit an offense against the Buddha and cannot be said to have truly made offerings to the Buddhas.

If there is a son of good family who, upon hearing this discourse on the Tathāgata’s true virtues, develops pure faith and offers praise, their merit shall exceed that of the former by more than a hundred thousandfold; such a person performs a truly authentic offering.
"Good sons!
If you have pure faith in my heart, you should carefully copy and uphold this sutra; wherever this sutra resides, there all Buddhas dwell."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Jyotirasa, Vidyutkeśa, Nityaprabha, Viśuddhacakṣus, Maitreya, Abhayakara, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Mañjuśrī, Vadipūrṇa, Vadivikrama, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Prabhākara, and Samantabhadra—these eighty-four koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand leading Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"In the future, during the final age, we shall widely disseminate such sutras as these, causing all sentient beings to realize Great Nirvana.
World-Honored One!
Those who have not long planted roots of goodness will not have such a sutra enter their ears."
If there are those who receive, uphold, and widely disseminate this sutra, the praise of their merit would not be exhausted even in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
You all should thus revere the Buddha’s teachings and uphold the True Dharma.”

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Vijaya-śrī, along with the entire great assembly of devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Mahāvaipulya Siṃhanāda Sūtra
